title: Contemplation to attain love
hookLine: love shows itself in deeds; take, Lord, receive

lines: MORE IN DEEDS THAN IN WORDS.
cards: After the fourth week, the Exercises turn to a contemplation, and Ignatius opens it with two short remarks before any prayer at all. First: love ought to show itself more in deeds than in words. Second: love is a sharing.
The lover gives the beloved what they have, and the beloved gives back. Two sentences, plain as a kitchen table. No grand theory of love.
Everything that follows hangs from them, including a short prayer of offering, written right into the text.

teach.h: LOOK BACK AT WHAT YOU'VE BEEN GIVEN.
teach.b: The contemplation to attain love asks the person to look back over everything received. Creation. Redemption.

The particular gifts of one's own life: the people, the chances, the mercies. Ignatius says to ponder how much God has done, and how God wants to give, as far as possible, God's own self. Then the two remarks come back.

teach.h: IF LOVE IS SHARING, WHAT GOES BACK?
teach.b: If love is a sharing, and God has given this much, what does a person give back? Ignatius answers with a prayer, offered as if by someone moved by great love. It's known by its first Latin word, Suscipe: receive.
In substance it goes like this.
Take, Lord, receive all my liberty, my memory, my understanding, my whole will, everything I have and possess. You gave it to me; I give it back. It's all yours; dispose of it as you will.

Give me only your love and your grace; that is enough for me. Look at what is offered: not money, not a list of good works, but freedom, memory, mind and will, the very things the Exercises have been training all along.
Indifference, discernment, the choice made from the end. All of it, handed back. And what is asked in return: only love and grace.
The First Letter of John, in the Douay-Rheims, makes the same point about deeds: "let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth." So the Suscipe is not meant to stay a sentence.

how: The Suscipe closes the Spiritual Exercises' contemplation to attain love; some who pray in the Ignatian way say it at the end of a retreat, and some pray it daily.

o: Ignatius's prayer handing everything back to God

games.q: the contemplation to attain love — tap the pairs.
p: shown more in deeds than in words

s: Ignatius says love shows itself more in deeds than in words
his first remark, before the contemplation begins.
the Suscipe offers God money and good works
it offers liberty, memory, understanding and will.
the Suscipe asks God for many gifts in return
only love and grace: that, it says, is enough.

games.q: you've looked back over everything you've been given. Ignatius says love is a sharing. what does the person praying do next?
o: make a list of what's still missing.
offer back freedom, memory, mind and will.
games.why: the Suscipe: take, Lord, receive. everything is handed back, and only love and grace are asked for.

practice: Let your hands rest open. If you know the Suscipe, pray it slowly, a phrase on each breath; if not, use today's line, take, Lord, receive, and name one at a time what Ignatius offers: my freedom, my memory, my mind, my will.
If you don't pray, sit with the question underneath it: what am I holding that I could hand over?

wordCard.voice: Suscipe. Receive: the first word of Ignatius's prayer of offering, which hands back freedom, memory, mind and will, and asks only for love and grace. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: receive, take up. the prayer is named for its first word.

carryVoice: Your line: take, Lord, receive. Love shows itself more in deeds than in words. Back tomorrow, same hill.
